item.title: On the Nonemptiness of the Core: Connecting Cooperative Games and Asset Pricing
item.description: arXiv:2611.13189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the Bondareva--Shapley theorem for infinite cooperative games can be derived from a version of the fundamental theorem of asset pricing. The link is the Choquet extension of a game, viewed as a possibly nonlinear pricing rule on the space of measurable simple payoffs. Under this identification, balancedness translates into no arbitrage, and a linear functional dominated by the pricing rule yields an allocation in the anti-core; the core statement follows by duality. Applying the arbitrage-free pricing theorem of Cornet (2025), we recover the characterization of the nonvacuity of the core initiated by Schmeidler (1967) and established in full generality by Bartl and Pinter (2023) for bounded-below games. Unlike the earlier derivation in Cornet (2025), our argument does not require the game to have bounded variation or the collection of coalitions to be a $\sigma$-algebra.
item.dc:creator: Bernard Cornet, Mikl\'os Pint\'er

item.title: Choosing Complexity: Cognitive Ability, Overconfidence, and Task Choice
item.description: arXiv:2611.13259v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Workers and organizations routinely choose between complex tasks that differ in their success-payment tradeoff. We study how cognitive ability and overconfidence shape this choice of task complexity, both theoretically and experimentally. Consistent with our model, we find that more cognitively able individuals choose more complex tasks. Conditional on cognitive ability, we find that more overconfident individuals also choose more complex tasks. In about 75% of the decisions, subjects pick their payoff-maximizing task, and higher cognitive ability is weakly associated with more efficient choices of task complexity. But errors are strikingly one-sided: those who fail to choose optimally pick tasks that are too complex. Our findings suggest that organizations should pair task menus and incentives for choosing more complex tasks with information and feedback that help workers assess their ability and probability of success. This preserves the benefits of self-selection while reducing costly overreach.
item.dc:creator: David Gill, Zhongheng Qiao

item.title: Feedback Design in the Shadow of Strategic Communication
item.description: arXiv:2611.13450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study optimal feedback design when evaluations affect subsequent strategic communication within organizations. A firm designs public feedback about an employee's potential before the employee communicates private information about project-specific circumstances to a manager. While more informative feedback helps the manager make better decisions, it can also intensify preference conflicts and undermine the credibility of subsequent communication. We characterize the optimal feedback policy. First, full disclosure is either optimal for all prior beliefs or strictly suboptimal for all of them. In particular, it is optimal when preference conflicts are sufficiently small or sufficiently large. Second, when full disclosure is suboptimal, no disclosure is optimal for some priors, while partial disclosure is strictly optimal for some priors if and only if the number of messages in equilibrium communication varies with posterior beliefs. Third, optimal partial disclosure can conclusively identify low-potential employees when high potential is rare, but high-potential employees when it is common.
item.dc:creator: Daiki Kishishita, Tomoki Tsujita

item.title: Obvious Group Manipulations and Top Trading Cycles
item.description: arXiv:2611.13469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a group version of non-obvious manipulability, which is stronger than the original definition by Troyan and Morrill (2020) and weaker than group strategy-proofness, and study its implications in Shapley-Scarf housing markets. We provide several characterizations of the Top Trading Cycles mechanism using the new condition.
item.dc:creator: Ryoga Doi, Kazumasa Ikeda, Kensei Nakamura

item.title: Herding with Multiple States: When the Prior Matters
item.description: arXiv:2611.13632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In sequential observational learning with more than two states, the same information structure and preferences can yield learning for some full-support priors and herding for others. This disproves a conjecture of Kartik, Lee, Liu, and Rappoport (2024, working-paper version). In the counterexample, the cascade region has nonempty interior, yet learning occurs for generic full-support priors outside it. Focusing on information and preferences, we introduce two necessary conditions for learning. Escapability requires that signals can provide arbitrarily strong evidence that any given action is ex post suboptimal; pairwise escapability is its pairwise variant. If escapability fails, herding occurs for some initial prior; if pairwise escapability fails, it occurs for every full-support prior. For a class of environments with interval optimality and monotone likelihood ratios, escapability completely characterizes learning and herding independently of the full-support initial prior. With location-shift signals, this characterization reduces to pairwise distinguishability, a generalization of unbounded beliefs (Smith and S{\o}rensen, 2000).
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Chen

item.title: The invisible hand as an emergent property
item.description: arXiv:2508.14498v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a multi-sector competitive economy where firms reallocate across sectors under myopic profit-seeking behaviour and quadratic reallocation costs. The dynamic path, formalised as a gradient flow in Wasserstein space, yields two emergent properties: (i) short-run equilibria can be seen as solutions to sequential aggregate optimisation problems; and (ii) the long-run equilibrium is globally stable and efficient. Linearizing around the common long-run equilibrium, we show that convergence can be faster or slower under a planner who accounts for reallocation costs than under decentralized adjustment.
item.dc:creator: Giorgio Fabbri, Davide Fiaschi, Cristiano Ricci

item.title: Designing Markets for Screening: Optimal Composition and the Geometry of Surplus
item.description: arXiv:2604.09340v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We characterize the structure of market compositions that generate Pareto efficient outcomes and the geometry of the surplus set in a screening model with type-dependent costs. Under mild cost-curvature conditions, agent-oriented optima use rather than suppress screening to sustain information rents: all agents are served, allocations strictly separate types, and an atom at the highest type receives the efficient allocation. Each Pareto efficient payoff is implemented by a unique market. When costs are type independent or a type with no gains from trade is feasible, we also characterize the entire surplus set and establish its convexity. Otherwise, type-dependent costs can generate nonconvexity. Market segmentation can expand attainable outcomes only on the rent-suppression side of the set, without increasing maximum agent surplus at any level of principal surplus. The characterization and comparative statics link market formation to the distribution of surplus and identify the limits on payoffs attainable under screening.
item.dc:creator: Panagiotis Kyriazis

item.title: Coordination Mechanisms with Partially Specified Probabilities
item.description: arXiv:2605.07469v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A mediator coordinates play in a finite game, but instead of revealing a fully known correlation device it discloses only some statistics of the process that generates players' private messages. Players complete the partially specified process by minimizing a loss over the set of distributions consistent with what is disclosed: maximum Shannon entropy is the leading case, and the analysis covers every strictly convex and symmetric loss that never excludes an event the data do not exclude. We obtain four sets of results. (i) With unrestricted message spaces, the implementable outcomes are exactly the jointly coherent outcomes, namely distributions supported on the support of the set of correlated equilibria. (ii) The characterization is unchanged when players' partial knowledge also concerns the joint distribution of messages and actions, whether or not players know the strategy profile. (iii) Under direct implementation, implementability depends on the loss and reduces to a single optimality condition linking the outcome to some correlated equilibrium: among all distributions on the line joining the equilibrium and the outcome, the equilibrium must be the one with the lowest loss. (iv) In single-agent decision problems the designer can induce, with probability one, any action that is a best response to some interior belief.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Giordano

item.title: Bundling Complements
item.description: arXiv:2607.07982v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I study a monopolist selling goods to a buyer with combinatorial preferences. The dual of the seller's problem is a minimum-cost flow of the differential virtual value. I characterize when the type distribution alone determines the differential virtual value. The distribution then determines the *required directions*, along which the dual transports mass, and the preference determines the *covered directions* of each bundle; optimality is full coverage. This separation enables comparative statics in the preference: raising a complementarity premium on bundles containing a core of goods widens their covered directions. Two premium thresholds describe the optimum: above a lower threshold the grand bundle must be offered; above an upper threshold a *core-peripheral* menu --- a bundled core with optional add-ons not sold standalone --- is optimal, and every optimal menu is core-peripheral. The upper threshold is finite if and only if the menu is *inclusive*: it excludes no near-top buyer.
item.dc:creator: Weijie Zhong

item.title: Observable Self-Restraint in Repeated Cheap Talk
item.description: arXiv:2610.33390v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A long-lived sender seeks to persuade short-lived receivers, who cannot verify his past advice, to take his preferred action. Restrictions on recommendation histories alone can support a partially informative equilibrium. Under rolling quotas, which cap favorable recommendations within a fixed memory window, a partial order on histories ranks the cost of favorable advice. When receivers infer the reason for a violation, they can still follow the violating recommendation, so state sequences can lead the sender to exceed the quota, ending informative communication on the equilibrium path. As the sender becomes patient, suitable rolling quotas approach his normalized equilibrium payoff ceiling.
item.dc:creator: Haohui Wang
